newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire opposes refugee aid on its soil.
newsitem.headline: Zaire opposes refugee aid on its soil.

text.p: Zaire served notice on Wednesday it will stop aid agencies using its soil to distribute food for more than a million stranded refugees from Rwanda and Burundi.
Government spokesman Boguo Makeli also said multi-national plans to save the refugees must not obscure Zaire's call for the Rwandan army to quit territory Zaire accuses it of occupying.

"We are asking humanitarian organisations to stop distributing any aid to the refugees on Zairean soil," Boguo told Reuters. "They must instead distribute aid in Rwanda and Burundi so that the refugees can receive it, having travelled along the humanitarian corridors that have been discussed."
France and Spain have proposed an international force to come to the rescue of the Hutu refugees dispersed from camps by two weeks of fighting between Zaire's army and ethnic Tutsis.

Zaire accuses its eastern neighbours of backing the rebels. It boycotted a summit of seven regional leaders in Kenya on Tuesday which urged the United Nations to arrange a neutral force to come to the rescue of refugees.
Boguo said his government had not received details of the Nairobi summit and could not comment until it did.
"Our objective is that the refugees return home and that we recover the territory which has been taken from us," Boguo said. "The means to achieve this must not obscure that objective."
Asked if Zaire would accept the planned intervention force, Boguo, who is information minister, said: "The issue will have to be negotiated when we are in full possession of the details."

Half-Tutsi Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, who is accused by Zairean militants of softness in dealing with ethnic Tutsi rebels, had said there can be no negotitaions as long as Zairean territory is "under occupation".
But the scenario may have changed since ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko moved from cancer treatment in Switzerland to his retreat in southern France and appeared to take control.
Mobutu has dominated Zaire during more than 30 years in power and is able to cut deals with neigbours or enemies in a way no other Zairean can.
A U.N. special envoy arrived in France on Wednesday for talks with Mobutu on the conflict, which has triggered Africa's worst refugee crisis since the 1994 Rwanda massacres.
Boguo challenged Rwanda to honour its promise of welcoming the 1.1 million Hutus who fear revenge for the genocide of up to a million Tutsis in 1994. Tutsis now rule Rwanda.
"The Rwandan regime has said it will accept the return of the refugees. We hope this time they are sincere and that their declaration will be followed by concrete actions," he said.
Rwandan Foreign Minister Anastase Gasana said on Tuesday Rwanda would strongly oppose any international military intervention in eastern Zaire but would welcome the Hutus.

"We wish that in spite of everything (the refugees) return to Rwanda. The Rwandan government is ready to do everything to facilitate the return of the refugees," Gasana told a news conference in Brussels.
Aid agencies say they have no precise idea of where the refugees are since fighting forced them to flee camps in eastern Zaire and aid workers looking after them were evacuated.

In Kinshasa dozens of students wearing white bandanas gathered outside their college on Wednesday, stopping cars and demanding money for the burial of a student killed in protests the previous day, witnesses said.
The government has banned all protests mainly to head off a witchhunt of ethnic Tutsis, hundreds of whom have fled to neighbouring Congo. Many are missing or in hiding, Tutsis say.
